issues.description: is_registered mutation on shared TritonLoraConfig is a race-prone place-oriented hack
issues.detail: TritonLoraConfig instances are shared across all concurrent requests for a model (stored once in model_metadata). _create_trtllm_generate_request reads is_registered, conditionally loads weights from disk, then mutates is_registered = True. Under concurrent first requests for the same LoRA, multiple coroutines will all see is_registered=False, all load and send weights, and the flip is non-atomic. This complects three concerns into one mutable place: identity (which LoRA), value (the weights/config arrays), and time (has the backend cached this yet). The cache state belongs in a separate, explicit registry keyed by (model, lora_name, task_id) with proper synchronization, not as a mutable boolean glued onto a config record.

issues.description: LoRA weights loaded from disk on every cold request inside the hot path
issues.detail: np.load of model.lora_weights.npy and model.lora_config.npy happens synchronously inside _create_trtllm_generate_request, on the request-serving path, with no caching of the loaded arrays. Even ignoring the is_registered race, the value (the weight tensor) and the act of materializing it from a place (the file) are complected with request construction. The weights are values: load them once at parse time, hold them as values, and pass them by reference. Disk IO in an async request handler is incidental complexity that the design invited by not separating loading from sending.

issues.description: _parse_lora_configs complects two different backends in one branching function
issues.detail: What used to be _get_vllm_lora_names (a function that answers one question for one backend) is now a single function with an `if backend == "vllm": ... else: ...` ladder that does different file probing, different validation, and different return-record construction. The two cases share almost no code beyond the directory walk. This is the classic complecting pattern: one name, two concepts. Decompose into _parse_vllm_lora_configs and _parse_trtllm_lora_configs, with a tiny dispatcher. The shared part (resolving the version directory) is the only thing worth factoring, and it should be its own pure function returning a value.

issues.description: task_id assignment is implicit, mutable, and depends on dict iteration order
issues.detail: lora_task_id is a counter incremented as multi_lora.json is walked. The task_id assigned to a given LoRA name is therefore a function of (a) the order of keys in a JSON object and (b) the order of repo_paths. That is place-oriented identity assignment: the same logical LoRA may get different task_ids across restarts or repo layouts, and there is no guarantee of stability or uniqueness across multiple models that share a backend. Make task_id an explicit value derived from a stable input (e.g., a hash of the name, or an explicit field in multi_lora.json), or document the lifetime/scope of task_id as 'per-process, per-model' and prove that's what the backend expects.

issues.description: Stray debug print('backend: ...') and traceback prints left in production code
issues.detail: _parse_lora_configs has a `print(f"backend: {backend}")` inside the per-LoRA loop, and all three FastAPI routers now print full tracebacks on every ServerError/Exception. This is debugging scaffolding being shipped as code. It complects logging policy (where, at what level, with what fields) with control flow, and it will dump tracebacks to stdout on every transient backend hiccup. Use a logger with a configured level, or remove. The router prints in particular look like 'easy' (familiar) instead of 'simple' (a single logging concept owned by one place).

issues.description: TritonLoraConfig is both an immutable spec and a mutable cache record
issues.detail: The dataclass holds name/task_id/path (immutable facts about a configured LoRA) alongside is_registered (a mutable fact about whether this process has sent the weights to the backend yet). Those are two different values with two different time semantics. Mixing them in one record is the textbook complecting of value and identity-over-time. Split into TritonLoraSpec (frozen) and a separate registration registry that maps spec -> registered? with appropriate synchronization.

issues.description: _get_lora_config can return None despite annotation TritonLoraConfig
issues.detail: The method is annotated `-> TritonLoraConfig` but explicitly `return None` when lora_name is None or metadata has no configs. Callers treat None as a sentinel meaning 'no LoRA'. The type is lying about the value. Either annotate Optional[TritonLoraConfig] and let callers branch on it explicitly, or have two separate functions (one that requires a LoRA, one that doesn't). Right now the type is incidental noise that contradicts the runtime contract.

issues.description: Duplicate LoRA-name validation logic in three places
issues.detail: _validate_chat_request, _validate_completion_request, and _get_lora_config all independently scan metadata.lora_configs for a name match and raise ClientError on miss. Three copies of the same lookup, three places that have to stay in sync, three list comprehensions doing the same O(n) scan. The value 'which LoRA does this name resolve to' is a single concept; it should be one pure function (probably returning Optional[TritonLoraConfig]) reused everywhere, with a single error message. Bonus: build a dict keyed by name once at parse time so lookups are O(1) and not a comprehension over a list.

Annotation says `None | List[tuple[str, str]]` but the function returns `List[TritonLoraConfig]`. A small thing, but type annotations are values that document intent; a wrong one is worse than none. Fix to `Optional[List[TritonLoraConfig]]`.

issues.description: lora_config_path local name shadowed inside the loop
issues.detail: `lora_config_path` is set once outside the backend branch as the path to multi_lora.json, then reassigned inside the loop as the path to model.lora_config.npy. Two distinct values, same name. Mechanical, not load-bearing, but it's exactly the kind of place-oriented reuse that makes the code harder to read and that Hickey would flag as a tell that the function is doing too much.

issues.description: The TRT-LLM 'first request must include weights' protocol leaks into the frontend
issues.detail: The backend's caching protocol (send lora_task_id + lora_weights + lora_config the first time, lora_task_id alone thereafter) is implementation detail that the OpenAI frontend has now adopted as its own state machine. This is essential complexity of the backend protocol, but the right place to handle it is a thin TRT-LLM client adapter that owns the registration cache as a value (a set of task_ids known to the backend), not the request-construction function. The question that should have been asked first: 'whose job is it to know whether the backend has seen this LoRA before?' The current answer complects that job into the request builder.

issues.description: Silent `return None` on parse failure hides real errors
issues.detail: When the multi_lora.json read raises any non-ServerError exception, the code prints a traceback and returns None, which the caller interprets as 'this model has no LoRAs'. A malformed JSON file is silently equivalent to 'no LoRAs configured'. That conflates two very different facts (no config vs. broken config) into one value. Either raise, or return a tagged result (Ok([...]) | Err(reason)) so the caller can decide.

review.summary: The change adds a real capability (TRT-LLM multi-LoRA in the OpenAI frontend), and the parse/select shape is roughly right, but several concerns are complected in ways that will bite in production. The biggest issue is is_registered: a mutable boolean glued onto a shared config record, flipped from inside an async request handler that also does disk IO and weight transmission. That single line entangles value (the weights), identity (which LoRA), and time (has the backend been told yet), and it is not safe under concurrent first-touch requests for the same adapter. The cleaner decomposition is a frozen TritonLoraSpec, a registration registry owned by a thin TRT-LLM adapter, and weights loaded once as values at parse time rather than fetched from a place on each cold request. Secondary cleanups: split _parse_lora_configs by backend instead of branching, deduplicate the three copies of LoRA-name validation behind one lookup, fix the lying return-type annotations, make task_id assignment explicit rather than dict-iteration-order, and pull the debug prints and traceback-on-every-error scaffolding out of the routers and parser. The question that should have been asked first: whose job is it to know whether the backend has already seen this LoRA, and where does that fact live as a value?
